1. Realized portfolio value

Three books that all start at the same dollar: the curated one, a buy-and-hold of the starter_watchlist (AAPL, GOOGL, AMZN) bought equal-dollar on day 1 and never touched, and SPY. Squares mark the weekly rebalances — dark red where an event actually opened or closed, orange where the curator rebalanced but changed nothing. Over this window the curated book ended at $329,294, the starter basket at $106,530, SPY at $90,297 — curating beat the starter basket and SPY. Kept OUT of the headline on purpose: a backtest steered by returns on known history is how you overfit, which is why this page leads with breadth and precision.

2. Watchlist composition over time

One row per ticker. The pale bar is the span the curator kept it WATCHLISTED — it held the thesis; the solid bar is the span the optimizer actually FUNDED it. The gap between them is the honest part: a name the curator believed in and the math never backed. Colour is the ticker’s dominant BEAT — which part of the firehose its evidence came from. Grey means no beat-attributable evidence.

3. Cumulative $ gain per holding

The 5 best and 5 worst funded names, with every other name rolled into one grey bar. A result resting on one or two names is a different thing from the same return spread across many — and the difference is not visible in the equity curve above. Click any named bar for that ticker’s price history, with ▲/▼ marking the moments the optimizer funded and unfunded it.

4. Perfect-foresight ceiling per ticker

For each name, the best single buy→sell that was available INSIDE the span the curator held it watchlisted (pale), against what simply holding it start-to-finish returned (solid). No credit for names it never found. A LOW ceiling means the pick itself was a dud; a HIGH ceiling with a weak hold means the pick was fine and the timing was not. Hindsight upper bound — not attainable. Click any bar to open that ticker’s price history, with the watchlisted span shaded and the funded span drawn heavier.

5. Cumulative $ gain per beat

The same dollars as the panel above, rolled up to the BEAT that surfaced each ticker’s evidence — i.e. which part of the firehose paid. A beat that costs money is a retrieval-vocabulary problem, not a curator one.

6. Cumulative $ gain per event

The same gains grouped by the EVENT that motivated them. PWR groups this by wave bucket; GHR's unit of thesis is the event, so this is its analogue. It answers whether the curator's ideas paid, independently of which vehicle expressed them.

7. Portfolio $ by event over time

How the book was distributed across events as the year ran. Wide bands that persist mean concentrated conviction; a churn of thin bands means the optimizer kept rotating.

8. Allocation over time

Dollars held per ticker, stacked — the top edge is the portfolio value. The always_include anchors (SPY, GLD, BIL) sit outside the watchlist cap and are where idle capital parks; gaps are uninvested cash.

9. Curator funnel

Everything the curator touched, from the articles it read down to the picks it logged. The direct analogue of the firehose funnel — but here the interesting collapse is at the top: a whole week of articles yields a handful of candidates. Log x-axis.

10. Breadth over time

Events live, distinct tickers named, and how many separate catalysts those events represent — per rebalance. Several events on one theme is concentration wearing a diversity costume, which is why catalysts are drawn separately from events. The dashed line is max_watchlist = 6. Since the unfunded prune was turned on (2026-08-09) it binds in only 36 of 37 weeks — the prune keeps the live set under the cap by itself, so the cap is a backstop rather than an active knob. What used to sit between the solid and dashed lines was inventory the optimizer was never going to fund.

11. Scout inflow vs the cap

What the scout proposed each week against what it was allowed to admit (max_new_events, in investor_profile.backtest.md). If the proposal line sits below the cap, breadth is limited by the curator's judgement, not by the knob — and loosening the knob would change nothing.

12. Event timeline

Every event the curator opened. The pale bar spans proposed → terminated; the solid overlay is when the optimizer actually FUNDED it, coloured by beat. A bar with no solid section is a thesis the curator held and the math never backed.

13. Coverage vs picks, per ticker

Article counts for the 40 most-covered tickers in the corpus. Green got watchlisted at some point; grey was named in the news but never watchlisted.

14. Evidence by lede provenance

For every article the curator cited as evidence, where its text came from. If picks cluster on archived text the clean arm is earning its cost; if they cluster on live page text the corpus is leaning on look-ahead-biased material.

15. Evidence by source

Which outlets actually produced the articles behind the picks. Compare with the firehose dashboard's source panel: an outlet supplying much of the corpus but little of the evidence is volume without signal.

16. Evidence by beat

Which standing searches (retrieval_config.json) produced the articles behind the picks. A beat that fills the corpus but never appears here is paying rent without earning it.

17. Agent precision

Every thesis the curator held, and what that ticker returned over its live span — the standalone result of the idea, before any position sizing. This is the closest thing on this page to a skill measure: it asks whether the curator's calls were RIGHT, not whether the optimizer weighted them well. Green is profitable, red is not. Read it beside Breadth over time: breadth without precision is noise, precision without breadth is luck.

Each event's week-by-week journal: what the agent concluded, and why it eventually exited. Funded events first, then those that never held capital.
